questions.question: What does the `inline` modifier on a higher-order function like `fun <T> measure(block: () -> T): T` actually do?
options: The compiler pastes the body and lambda into each call site, so no lambda object is allocated
The lambda is compiled to a static singleton, so it is allocated once and reused on every call
It hints the JVM's JIT to inline the call at runtime; the generated bytecode is unchanged
It makes the function run on the caller's thread instead of a background thread
questions.explanation: `inline` is a compile-time transformation: the body of `measure` and the code of the lambda are pasted into the caller, so there is no `Function` object and no virtual `invoke()` call. Caching non-capturing lambdas as singletons is what happens WITHOUT `inline`, and the JIT plays no part in it.

questions.question: Which of these functions gains the most from being marked `inline`?
options: `fun <T> traced(name: String, block: () -> T): T`, a small wrapper used widely
`fun parseConfig(json: String): Config`, a 200-line parser with no lambda parameters
`fun add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = a + b`
`fun fib(n: Int): Int`, which calls itself recursively
questions.explanation: `inline` pays off when a function takes lambdas: it removes the lambda allocation and the `invoke()` call. With no function-type parameters the compiler warns that the gain is insignificant (the JIT inlines small methods anyway). A recursive function can't be inlined at all.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `return@tens 0` returns `0` from the lambda for that element, so `map` still produces three items. It doesn't skip the element, and it doesn't stop the whole `map` either.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because `measure` is inlined, the bare `return` exits `work` straight from the middle of `measure`'s pasted body. The `println("end")` after `block()` is skipped too, which is why wrappers that must always clean up use `try/finally`.

questions.explanation: It compiles and prints `4`. The compiler only gives a warning ("expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant"), because inlining a function with no lambda parameters saves almost nothing.

questions.question: Why doesn't this compile, and what's the fix?
options: An inlined lambda has no object to store; mark `block` as `noinline`
`block` might contain non-local returns; mark it `crossinline`
A top-level `var` can't hold a function type; make `saved` a `val`
Inline functions can't assign to properties; move the assignment out of `keep`
questions.explanation: An inline lambda parameter only exists as code pasted at the call site, so it can only be called or passed to another inline function. To store it (or pass it to a non-inline function) it must be a real object, which is what `noinline` gives you. `crossinline` lambdas are still inlined, so storing one fails the same way.

questions.explanation: The non-local `return` leaves `save` from inside the inlined `try` block, and `finally` still runs on the way out, so `unlock` prints. `print("after")` is skipped because `save` has already returned.

questions.question: `doOnLayout` from core-ktx is declared as `inline fun View.doOnLayout(crossinline action: (View) -> Unit)`. What happens with this code in a Fragment?
options: Compile error: bare `return` isn't allowed in a `crossinline` lambda
It compiles, and `return` exits only the lambda
It compiles, but crashes if the view hasn't been laid out when `doOnLayout` is called
questions.explanation: `action` may run later from an `OnLayoutChangeListener`, after `onViewCreated` has returned, so it is `crossinline` and non-local returns are forbidden. Inline does not automatically mean bare `return` is allowed; you need `return@doOnLayout`.

questions.question: A 60-line function with one lambda parameter is marked `inline` and called from 300 places in an app. What is the main downside?
options: Its bytecode is copied into all 300 call sites, bloating the dex/APK size
A new `Function0` object is allocated on every one of the 300 calls
It can no longer be called from Java code
The lambda is evaluated lazily, only the first time the function runs
questions.explanation: Inlining duplicates the whole body at every call site, so large inline functions cause code bloat. Allocation is what `inline` removes, not what it adds. Java can still call an inline function; it just runs as a normal, non-inlined method.

questions.question: This compiles: inside a `crossinline` lambda a bare `return` is forbidden, but a labeled `return@post` is allowed.
questions.explanation: `crossinline` only bans non-local returns, the ones that would exit the caller's function. `return@post` just ends the lambda, which is safe even when the lambda runs inside a `Runnable` later.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `return@outer` ends the current call of the OUTER lambda, so for each `a` the inner loop stops at `b == 20` and `print("x ")` is skipped too. The outer `forEach` then moves on to the next `a`. It's not a return from `main`, so `end` prints.

questions.question: Why doesn't this compile?
options: An `inline` property can't have a backing field, so it can't have an initializer
`inline` can only be applied to functions, never to properties, since properties have no call site
Inline properties must be `val`; `inline var` is not allowed
An inline property's type must be a function type
questions.explanation: `inline` on a property inlines its getter/setter at the use site, so there must be no backing field (no initializer, no `field`). `inline val` and `inline var` with custom accessors are both allowed, and the type can be anything. Compute the value in a getter instead, e.g. `get() = raw * 2`.

questions.question: Inside a regular function `fun load() { ... }` with `items: List<Int>`, in which of these lambdas does a bare `return` compile?
questions.explanation: Non-local `return` works only in lambdas passed to inline functions: `forEach`, `List.map` and `run` are all inline. `Sequence.map` is NOT inline (it stores the lambda for lazy evaluation), and `Thread {}` and `lazy {}` keep the lambda to run later, so a bare `return` is prohibited in all three.

questions.question: What does this print with Kotlin 2.4?
options: Compile error: continue is not allowed inside a lambda
questions.explanation: Since Kotlin 2.2, non-local `break` and `continue` are stable inside lambdas passed to inline functions. `continue` targets the enclosing `for` loop, not the `forEach`, so it jumps straight to the next `i`, skipping `c` and the `print("| ")` too.

questions.question: `Logger` is in a library module. Which change makes this compile while keeping `tag` out of the library's public API?
options: Declare it as `@PublishedApi internal val tag = "T"`
Declare it as `@JvmField private val tag = "T"`
Mark the `m` parameter as `noinline` so the body isn't copied
questions.explanation: A public inline function's body is copied into other modules, so it can only touch public API. `@PublishedApi internal` makes `tag` callable from inlined code (it's public in bytecode) while Kotlin callers still see it as internal. Plain `internal` fails the same check, and `noinline` doesn't change the fact that the body reads `tag`.

questions.question: This fails with "cannot inline 'block' here: it might contain non-local returns". Which changes, each on its own, make it compile?
options: Change the call site to `post { println("posted"); return@post }`
questions.explanation: `block` is called inside a `Runnable`, another execution context, where a non-local return could not exit `main`. `crossinline` keeps it inlined but bans such returns. `noinline` or dropping `inline` turns it into a normal object. `invoke()` is the same call, and the error is in the declaration, so changing the call site doesn't help.
